q: Which products form when 2-methylbut-2-ene is treated with 1. O<sub>3</sub>, 2. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>S?
h: Cut the C=C and put a C=O on each carbon. Reductive workup stops at the aldehyde.
w: Ozonolysis cleaves the C=C; each alkene carbon becomes a C=O. The carbon bearing two methyls becomes acetone, and the CH carbon becomes acetaldehyde. Dimethyl sulfide is a reductive workup, so the aldehyde is not oxidized: acetone and acetaldehyde.
x: Acetic acid would form with an oxidative workup (H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) or hot KMnO<sub>4</sub>; (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>S leaves the aldehyde intact.
Butan-2-one and formaldehyde come from 2-methylbut-1-ene, whose C=C is at the end of the chain.
Propanal and acetaldehyde come from pent-2-ene, which has no branching methyl on the alkene carbon.

q: What is the product of this reaction?
h: When the C=C is in a ring, ozonolysis opens the ring and both carbonyls stay in one molecule.
w: Cleaving the ring C=C opens the ring into one chain. The methyl-bearing carbon becomes a ketone (CH3C=O) and the CH carbon becomes an aldehyde, with four CH2 groups in between: 6-oxoheptanal.
x: 6-Oxoheptanoic acid has a carboxylic acid; that needs an oxidative workup or hot KMnO<sub>4</sub>, not (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>S.
Cyclohexanone (plus formaldehyde) comes from methylenecyclohexane, whose C=C is outside the ring.
Heptane-2,6-dione would need methyl groups on both alkene carbons; the CH carbon becomes an aldehyde, not a ketone.

q: Alkene X (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>14</sub>) reacts with 1. O<sub>3</sub>, 2. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>S to give octane-2,7-dione (shown) as the only organic product. What is X?
h: One product containing two C=O groups from a C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>14</sub> alkene means a ring. Join the two carbonyl carbons back together with a C=C.
w: C8H14 has two degrees of unsaturation: one C=C and one ring. A single product with both carbonyls means the C=C was in a ring. Reconnecting the two ketone carbons (C2 and C7) with a double bond gives a six-membered ring with a methyl on each alkene carbon: 1,2-dimethylcyclohexene.
x: 1,3-Dimethylcyclohexene gives 2-methyl-6-oxoheptanal (one aldehyde), because one alkene carbon is a CH.
1-Methylcycloheptene gives 7-oxooctanal, a keto aldehyde, because one of its alkene carbons is a CH.
(2E,6E)-Octa-2,6-diene gives two acetaldehyde molecules and butanedial, three products instead of one.

q: What is the organic product of this reaction?
h: Hot, acidic KMnO<sub>4</sub> cleaves C=C, and any aldehyde formed is oxidized further.
w: Hot KMnO4 cleaves the C=C like ozonolysis, but the CH carbon is oxidized all the way to a carboxylic acid. The methyl-bearing carbon has no H, so it stops as a ketone: 6-oxoheptanoic acid.
x: 6-Oxoheptanal is the reductive ozonolysis product; hot KMnO<sub>4</sub> oxidizes the aldehyde to an acid.
The cis diol forms with cold, dilute, basic KMnO<sub>4</sub>; hot acidic KMnO<sub>4</sub> cleaves the C–C bond.
Hexanedioic acid would require cutting off the methyl carbon; a ketone carbon has no H and is not oxidized further.

q: An alkene C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> is heated with acidic KMnO<sub>4</sub>; the products are butan-2-one and CO<sub>2</sub>. What is the alkene?
h: CO<sub>2</sub> comes from a terminal =CH<sub>2</sub>. Rebuild the C=C from the ketone carbon.
w: A =CH2 group is oxidized all the way to CO2. The other alkene carbon became the C=O of butan-2-one, so it carried a methyl and an ethyl: 2-methylbut-1-ene.
x: 2-Methylbut-2-ene gives acetone and acetic acid; neither carbon is a =CH<sub>2</sub>.
Pent-1-ene gives butanoic acid and CO<sub>2</sub>; its internal alkene carbon is a CH, which becomes an acid, not a ketone.
Pent-2-ene gives acetic acid and propanoic acid; it has no =CH<sub>2</sub> to make CO<sub>2</sub>.

q: Compound Y (C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>12</sub>) gives heptanedioic acid, HO<sub>2</sub>C(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>5</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H, as the only product when heated with acidic KMnO<sub>4</sub>. What is Y?
h: All seven carbons stay in one product, and both ends are COOH. Where was the C=C?
w: The single product keeps all seven carbons, so the C=C was in a ring, and both alkene carbons were CH (each became a COOH). Joining the two acid carbons with a C=C gives a seven-membered ring: cycloheptene.
x: 1-Methylcyclohexene gives 6-oxoheptanoic acid; the methyl-bearing carbon becomes a ketone, not an acid.
Methylenecyclohexane gives cyclohexanone and CO<sub>2</sub>.
Hepta-1,6-diene gives pentanedioic acid plus two CO<sub>2</sub>; the terminal CH<sub>2</sub> carbons are lost.

q: Which reagents convert hex-1-ene into pentanal?
h: You need to cut the C=C and stop at the aldehyde.
w: Ozonolysis with a reductive workup cleaves the C=C into two carbonyl compounds and leaves aldehydes as aldehydes: hex-1-ene gives pentanal and formaldehyde. Answer: 1. O3, 2. (CH3)2S.
x: Hot KMnO<sub>4</sub> oxidizes the aldehyde further and gives pentanoic acid (and CO<sub>2</sub>).
OsO<sub>4</sub> adds two OH groups (hexane-1,2-diol) without breaking the C–C bond.
An H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> workup is oxidative and gives pentanoic acid.

q: Which reagents carry out this conversion?
h: The OH ends up on the less substituted alkene carbon.
w: The OH is on the former =CH2, the less substituted alkene carbon: anti-Markovnikov hydration. That is hydroboration–oxidation.
x: Acid-catalyzed hydration is Markovnikov and gives 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol.
Oxymercuration–demercuration is also Markovnikov and gives 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol.
Ozonolysis removes the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon as formaldehyde; reducing cyclohexanone then gives cyclohexanol, which has one fewer carbon.

q: Which sequence converts 3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene into 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene as the major product?
h: The skeleton must change. Which step rearranges it, and which base gives the more substituted alkene?
w: The target has a different carbon skeleton, so a rearrangement is needed. HBr gives the secondary cation, which undergoes a 1,2-methyl shift to the tertiary cation, giving 2-bromo-2,3-dimethylbutane. Ethoxide, a small base, then gives the Zaitsev (tetrasubstituted) alkene, 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene: 1. HBr, 2. NaOCH2CH3, heat.
x: tert-Butoxide is bulky and removes a primary CH<sub>3</sub> hydrogen, giving the Hofmann product 2,3-dimethylbut-1-ene as the major alkene.
With peroxides HBr adds anti-Markovnikov by a radical path with no rearrangement; the primary bromide then gives the ether or 3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene, never the new skeleton.
Oxymercuration–demercuration does not rearrange and gives 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol, not an alkene.

q:
Which of these alkene reactions go through a carbocation intermediate?
I. HBr (no peroxides)
II. H2O, H2SO4 (cat.)
III. 1. BH3·THF 2. H2O2, NaOH
IV. 1. Hg(OAc)2, H2O 2. NaBH4
h: Reactions that can rearrange go through free carbocations.
w: HBr addition and acid-catalyzed hydration both begin with protonation to give a carbocation, which is why both can rearrange. Hydroboration is concerted, and oxymercuration goes through a bridged mercurinium ion instead of a free carbocation. Answer: I and II only.
x: Oxymercuration goes through a bridged mercurinium ion, not a free carbocation; that is why it does not rearrange.
HBr addition (I) does go through a carbocation, and oxymercuration (IV) does not.
Hydroboration is a concerted syn addition and oxymercuration uses a bridged ion; neither has a free carbocation.

q: What is the product when (E)-hex-3-ene is treated with 1. mCPBA, 2. H3O+?
c: A 1:1 mixture of meso and racemic hexane-3,4-diol
h: Epoxidation then acid opening is an anti addition. Combine anti with trans.
w: mCPBA gives the trans epoxide, and water opens the protonated epoxide with inversion at one carbon: overall anti addition of two OH groups. Anti addition to a trans alkene with identical ends gives the unlike (3R,4S) product: meso-hexane-3,4-diol.
x: The racemic (R,R)/(S,S) diol comes from syn dihydroxylation (OsO4) of this E alkene, or anti addition to the Z alkene.
Achiral reactants cannot give a single enantiomer, and the anti addition to the E alkene gives the meso diastereomer anyway.
Epoxidation and acid opening are both stereospecific, so only one diastereomer forms.

q:
Which statements about epoxidation of alkenes with mCPBA are correct?
I. The oxygen is transferred in a single concerted step.
II. A cis alkene gives a cis epoxide.
III. A carbocation intermediate forms, so methyl and hydride shifts can occur.
IV. More highly substituted (more electron-rich) alkenes react faster.
h: The peroxy acid is an electrophile, and the reaction has no intermediate.
w: mCPBA transfers O in one concerted step (I), so the alkene geometry is kept (II) and no cation forms to rearrange (III is false). The peroxy acid is electrophilic, so electron-rich, more substituted alkenes react faster (IV). Answer: I, II and IV only.
x: Statement IV is also true: alkyl groups make the π bond more nucleophilic toward the electrophilic peroxy acid.
Statement III is false; the concerted mechanism has no carbocation and no rearrangement.
Statement III is false, and statement II (stereospecific, cis stays cis) is true.

q: Br2 is added separately to (E)-but-2-ene and to (Z)-but-2-ene. How is the product from the E alkene related to either product from the Z alkene?
h: Work out each product first: anti addition to E and to Z.
w: Anti addition to the E alkene gives meso-(2R,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane; anti addition to the Z alkene gives racemic (2R,3R)/(2S,3S). The meso compound and either chiral enantiomer are stereoisomers that are not mirror images: diastereomers.
x: A meso compound is its own mirror image, so it cannot be the enantiomer of a chiral compound.
The reaction is stereospecific: the two alkene isomers give different stereoisomers.
Both products are 2,3-dibromobutane, so the connectivity is the same.

q: Limonene is treated with excess O<sub>3</sub>, then (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>S. Besides formaldehyde, what is the organic product?
h: Both C=C bonds react with excess O<sub>3</sub>. The ring C=C opens the ring; the side-chain C=CH<sub>2</sub> loses its CH<sub>2</sub>.
w: Both alkenes are cleaved. The ring C=C opens: the methyl-bearing carbon becomes a methyl ketone and the CH carbon an aldehyde. The isopropenyl group loses CH2 as formaldehyde and becomes an acetyl group. Product: 3-acetyl-6-oxoheptanal (C9H14O3).
x: With excess O<sub>3</sub> the side-chain C=C is also cleaved; leaving it intact ignores the second alkene.
(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>S is a reductive workup; the aldehyde is not oxidized to a carboxylic acid.
With excess O<sub>3</sub> the ring C=C is also cleaved, so the ring does not survive.

q: An alkene C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub> gives propanoic acid as the only product when heated with acidic KMnO<sub>4</sub>. What is the alkene?
h: A single product means the two halves of the alkene are identical.
w: Each CH alkene carbon becomes a COOH. Two identical propanoic acid molecules mean the alkene was symmetric, CH3CH2CH=CHCH2CH3: hex-3-ene (either isomer gives the same product; the E isomer is shown).
x: 2-Methylpent-2-ene gives acetone and propanoic acid: the carbon with two methyls becomes a ketone.
2,3-Dimethylbut-2-ene gives only acetone, a ketone, because neither alkene carbon carries an H.
Hex-1-ene gives pentanoic acid and CO<sub>2</sub>.

q: What is the first intermediate formed when 2-methylbut-2-ene reacts with H<sub>2</sub>O and catalytic H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
h: The first step is protonation of the C=C. Which carbon should get the proton?
w: H+ adds to the CH carbon so that the positive charge ends up on the carbon bearing two methyls: the tertiary 2-methylbutan-2-yl cation. Water then traps it.
x: The secondary cation forms only if H<sup>+</sup> adds to the more substituted carbon, which is the less favorable choice.
The primary cation is not formed by protonating this alkene; it would be far less stable anyway.
A carbanion would need a nucleophile to attack the alkene; in acid the alkene is the nucleophile.

q: Pent-4-en-1-ol reacts with Br<sub>2</sub> in CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> (no water present) to give a cyclic product, C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>9</sub>BrO. What is it? (It forms as a racemate; one structure is drawn without stereochemistry.)
h: The molecule carries its own nucleophile. Which carbon of the bromonium ion does the OH attack, and what ring size results?
w: Br2 forms a bromonium ion on C4–C5. The OH group, held in the same molecule, attacks the more substituted carbon C4 (the one that carries more δ+), forming a five-membered ring, then loses H+. Br stays on C5: 2-(bromomethyl)oxolane (2-(bromomethyl)tetrahydrofuran).
x: Attack at the terminal CH<sub>2</sub> would form a six-membered ring, but that carbon carries less δ+ and the five-membered ring closes faster.
The dibromide forms when no internal nucleophile competes; here the OH captures the bromonium ion intramolecularly, and the product formula has only one Br.
The formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>9</sub>BrO requires a ring; this open-chain bromohydrin would be C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>11</sub>BrO<sub>2</sub> and needs water.

q: Which reaction gives a product that is a racemic mixture?
h: Draw each product and look for an internal mirror plane.
w: Br2 adds anti to cyclohexene, giving trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane, which is chiral; both enantiomers form equally, so the product is racemic (cyclohexene + Br2). The other three reactions give achiral meso products.
x: Anti addition to the E alkene gives meso-2,3-dibromobutane, which is achiral.
Syn dihydroxylation of the Z alkene gives meso-butane-2,3-diol, which is achiral.
Syn dihydroxylation of cyclohexene gives cis-cyclohexane-1,2-diol, a meso compound.

q: What is the major product of this reaction?
h: Add H to the alkene carbon that already has more hydrogens.
w: Protonation of the CH carbon gives the tertiary 1-methylcyclohexyl cation; chloride adds to it, giving 1-chloro-1-methylcyclohexane (Markovnikov addition).
x: 1-Chloro-2-methylcyclohexane would come from the less stable secondary cation (anti-Markovnikov regiochemistry).
(Chloromethyl)cyclohexane puts Cl on the methyl carbon, which was not part of the C=C.
1-Methylcyclohexan-1-ol is the hydration product; HCl adds H and Cl, not H and OH.
